lesson.title: Decisions and debugging
lesson.subtitle: If, then, else, and finding bugs

video.title: Decisions and debugging: If, then, else, and finding bugs
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: My robot was meant to stop at the door. Instead it walked straight into the wall, every single time. My pupils groaned, then one of them shouted: it’s a bug, sir, let’s find it!
Today: decisions, and how to find and fix bugs.
Programs make decisions. If it is raining, then take an umbrella, else take a hat. The if part is a condition: a question whose answer is yes or no. The answer decides which steps run.
Some decisions need two conditions. The classroom fan goes on if it is hot AND someone is in the room. The alarm rings if the door OR the window opens. AND needs both; OR needs at least one.

You can teach decisions with no device at all. Draw a flowchart on the board: boxes for actions, a diamond for each question. Pupils follow it with their fingers. Then play Simon says, with ifs: if you are wearing blue, stand up.

Now, bugs. A bug is a mistake in a program that makes it do the wrong thing. Debugging is finding and fixing it. Every programmer writes bugs, every day. The skill isn’t avoiding them; it’s finding them calmly.
Quick check! My robot should go forward two, turn right, forward one. My program says forward two, turn left, forward one. Which card is the bug?
The second card: it turns left instead of right. Notice how we found it. We compared what we wanted with what happened, card by card, and stopped at the first difference.
Give pupils a routine they can follow every time. Test the program and watch what happens. Find the first step that goes wrong. Change one thing only. Then test again, and repeat until it works.
Make bugs normal in your classroom. Celebrate a bug found, not just a program that works. Say I made a bug, out loud, when you make one. Pupils who aren’t afraid of bugs keep trying.
In the app, open Logic gates. Flip switches to learn AND and OR, then solve the Fan. Each cross in the table is a case your gates get wrong: change one gate at a time, and test again.
Your turn. A pupil’s robot crashes, and she wants to rewrite the whole program. What should she do first?
Find the first wrong step. Remember: a decision runs steps only if a condition is true. AND needs both conditions; OR needs one. Debugging is a routine: test, find, change one thing, test again.
Try it in class tomorrow: bug swap. Pairs write a robot program on paper with one bug hidden in it. They swap, find the other pair’s bug, and explain how they found it.

checkpoints.prompt: Wanted: forward 2, turn right, forward 1. Program: forward 2, turn left, forward 1. Which card is the bug?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the turn goes the wrong way. Fix that one card and test again.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — compare card by card: the second card turns left instead of right.

checkpoints.prompt: A pupil’s robot crashes and she wants to rewrite it all. What first?

options.text: Run it, find the first wrong step

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — find the first wrong step, change one thing, test again.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — rewriting or changing many cards hides the bug. Find the first wrong step first.
